paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I didn't translate this one, I'm sorry — you can take a picture of it. There's a question that comes up: people ask, why can't you remember between lives? I don't know if this answers the question, but it's a cool chart to think about and meditate on. So basically there are four types of beings here. The ones on the right: all the beings born of eggs — and you can put beings born of a womb in there as well, generally speaking. Normal beings — not Buddhas, not self-made Buddhas, not wheel-powered emperors.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I know not all of you can read it in English, I'm sorry, but it says entering, staying, and issuing. Entering means entering the womb. Staying means staying in the womb. And issuing means leaving the womb. So there are three different types of beings here. World wheel-powered emperors — people who have tremendous power over the world. Their seeds are so good that they can almost choose, and remember, going into the womb — from death into the womb. But once they're in there, they forget their previous life. And of course they don't remember it when they come out either. Still, they have this natural power in the world. There are just some people who have natural leadership. Someone I'd put in this category — I don't know if you know Dr. Wu. If you know him: he just has this way of bringing thousands of people together, and they just kind of follow him, like, "this guy's cool." They just have this natural thing where people want to follow them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The next category is called self-made Buddhas — which are neither self-made nor Buddhas. Basically, it's a particular level of realization you reach on the path. They can remember entering the womb, and they remember who they were while they're in the womb. But once they pop out, they don't remember. Now Buddhas, on the other hand, do all three: they enter, stay, and go — and they remember all of it. And those of us who are none of those three just forget. It has to do with a particular kind of karma that someone has. That's something to think about for a little bit: why would some people remember and some not? So you can think about it.

chapters.title: The Craving Spirits — Where the Teaching Comes From

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, next PowerPoint, Brian — slide number two. Next slide. We're now going to go deeper into the life of the craving spirits and the animals. We talked about what's above us, and we talked about what's below — and we're going to spend more time on what's below, because it's a lot easier to go there. The negativities in our minds are driving this more; the negative things in our consciousness are the main thing, so they easily pull us down. You only have to worry about the other ones if you have really, really good virtue and it's all ripening for you. Meditation is always good — but if you're someone who never gets angry and your meditation is always excellent, make sure you have a teacher and talk to them about it, so you don't go too far. But for the most part, if you suffer from any of the major afflictions — pride, jealousy, anger — is there anyone here who doesn't have any of those, in any form whatsoever? If you're honest, you probably do — if you are who you look like you are. If you have any of those things, this is the part to really focus on.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what are we going to be studying? All of this information actually comes from a different text — a text called the Tenrin Chonyi. I'm sorry, I just puked my words all over my face. It comes from the Tenrim Chenmo [BSTAN RIM CHEN MO], "The Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching." And it's via the Kadampa Geshe {? Cholomba}, who lived about 1250 AD to 1350 AD. We don't know the exact dates. And this book became the foundation for Je Tsongkapa's great Lam Rim, called the Lamrim Chenmo. Okay — that's just for your homework.

chapters.title: Hoping for Miserable Things — the Lottery

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, next slide. Let's talk about the hungry ghosts. Really cute, right? Try to imagine — the causes to get to this type of being are things a lot of us might already have in part within us. They say these beings were misled by their own — you don't know that word — frugality. By their own cheapness. They have a desire for the miserable things in life, or they're overwhelmed by a hope for the miserable things that people could give them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What do we mean by "the hope for miserable things"? I'll give you an example. Yesterday Brian and I were out for lunch — I bought the lunch. Was it lunch? It may have been lunch. It was at the greatest coffee shop in Taipei. And after lunch they handed me a ticket, and he goes, "here's your lottery ticket." Lottery ticket? Then he explained that Taiwan has this cool system that encourages people to buy stuff: the more you buy, the more chances you have to win the lottery every couple of months. So people save all these little receipts, hoping they're going to win. It sounds fun, right? But if you really think about it — and it's beautifully generous of the Taiwanese government, I'm not making fun of it — how many people are just hoping, "I hope I win the lottery in July," or whenever it is? And then the numbers get pulled, and you get out your big pile of receipts, scan your QR code, and one by one: "nah... damn it... no." And how many have you accumulated after a couple of months? And your mind is occupied with saving these pieces of paper.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We had a lottery last week in the United States for one billion US dollars. How many people ran to the store to buy their five-dollar lottery ticket, hoping they'll be the one who finally wins? It's miserable — losing every single week, throwing money into nothing. Of course you can have different conceptions about it. But really, it's just gambling. And in Taiwan it's, "if you buy more, you might win, so go buy stuff." Spend more money hoping you'll win something.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: By the way, I gave the ticket to Brian. But I made him promise that if he wins, he has to give me half — or rather, if I win, I'm giving him half, but he has to give me the other half. Because I can't win it as a foreigner. Then there's another particular suffering. I said, "Brian, if you win this, you could buy a house." And he said, "No — the house costs way too much money in Taiwan." Even if he wins the jackpot — and he has to give me half — his half isn't nearly enough to buy anything. So it's not even really a lottery. See what I'm saying?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I've imagined: what if I won a billion dollars? I'll finally be happy. Really? Does money buy happiness? A lot of people who win the lottery become the most unfortunate people in the world. If I won a billion dollars, would you be friends with me because I'm a cool guy — or because "Tim's going to take me on his private jet everywhere"? The whole thing is: you're hoping for something that's already miserable, because you can't take the money with you anyhow. The pharaohs of Egypt put money into their tombs, thinking it would be there for them in the afterlife. Surprise — someone went in a thousand years later and stole all the gold. So you're hoping for something that's meaningless anyway, from that point of view.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And if you won the lottery — why would you win it? Because you bought a ticket at Helen's Cafe? No — because you gave away chocolates for 7-7, Valentine's Day. Because you were generous in the past. If you want to ripen all your seeds and win one billion dollars, good luck. I don't think any of us could handle a billion dollars — what would you do with it? But it comes from your generosity anyway. If I have the seeds for a billion dollars, it doesn't matter whether I win the lottery, gamble, or run a business — the seeds will ripen anyway.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Continuing on with the craving spirits: not only do they have the hope for miserable things, but because of this mentality they go, "I have to keep this for myself. Mine. My precious." They couldn't give. If someone came to me and said, "I need some chocolate, Tim" — "no, I need to keep this for myself. Maybe someday I'll win the lottery. But I don't have enough right now, so this is mine." Then you're holding on to things. And so they basically don't do any good deeds. They didn't provide for their children, and they didn't provide for their spouses. They didn't care for those they were responsible to care for. Their jealousy. Their attachment. And so you become a being who's totally obsessed with that. Mine.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We'll talk about what those beings look like, but the primary thing is: they become a being who actually can't get what they crave. The karma of not sharing with others and being attached to your things ripens as a being who can't get what they want. And this isn't limited to material things — it can also be mental. When you're so focused on yourself, when your internal world is so self-absorbed that it's always about me, me, me — "I feel terrible. No one supports me. I can't do this." All of those things turn into craving spirits. And I'm not making fun of them. But you know people who are depressed all the time — they're just thinking about themselves. They don't want to be; they can't control it. You can kind of start to see what happens to people, and you can almost predict where their next life is going to be. And it's painful to watch. I think anything you can do to help somebody start giving things away — giving to others, supporting others — helps. If you're trying to help someone who's insular, who's stuck by themselves, who won't leave the house, who's physically or mentally depressed, clinically or not... And we see people go from incredibly happy and all of a sudden flip — or the other way, too. Karma can change really fast. But if you really take the time to think about it: you could become one of those beings.
